blocks.text: Principles of Safe Prescribing

A comprehensive clinical reference for doctors, medical students, interns and other authorised healthcare professionals, covering safe prescribing, drug calculations, administration, interactions, contraindications, adverse effects and condition-specific treatment.

Our approach will combine Nigeria-focused clinical practice with WHO recommendations and relevant international guidance, including NICE, BNF and BNF for Children where applicable. We will identify differences between guidelines when they affect the choice of medicine, dose or duration.

The guide will progress systematically from prescribing fundamentals to drug calculations, individual drug monographs and treatment protocols in Medicine, Paediatrics, Obstetrics & Gynaecology, and Surgery.

Prescribing is the clinical process of selecting and authorising a medicine for a specific patient, taking into account the diagnosis, treatment objectives, expected benefits, potential harms, appropriate dose, route, frequency, duration and monitoring requirements.

A good prescription is not merely a list of medicines. It is a patient-specific treatment plan that includes how the medicine will be administered, how its effectiveness will be assessed, and what to do if complications occur.

blocks.title: By the end of this chapter, you should be able to:

items.text: Select an appropriate medicine based on the patient's diagnosis and clinical condition.
Choose the correct formulation, dose, route, frequency and duration.
Identify contraindications, precautions, allergies and clinically significant drug interactions.
Prevent medication errors, including calculation and administration errors.
Recognise when laboratory investigations or drug-level monitoring are required.
Prescribe safely in children, pregnancy, breastfeeding, older adults and patients with renal or hepatic impairment.
Counsel patients and document treatment decisions appropriately.
Recognise adverse drug reactions and initiate appropriate management.

blocks.text: Confirm diagnosis, severity, history, allergies and relevant investigations.
Define the intended clinical outcome and urgency of treatment.
Consider medicines, non-pharmacological options and patient-specific risks.
Specify medicine, formulation, dose, route, frequency and duration.
Verify the order, give the medicine safely and explain its use.
Assess response, toxicity, adherence and the need to modify or stop treatment.
The cycle repeats whenever the patient's condition changes, a new medicine is introduced, an adverse effect occurs or treatment fails.

subsections.subsection_title: 1.4 The seven-step approach to rational prescribing

blocks.text: The WHO Guide to Good Prescribing teaches a structured approach to selecting treatment, choosing a suitable medicine, writing the prescription, informing the patient and monitoring the outcome.
A useful clinical adaptation is the following seven-step method.
Define the patient's problem
Establish the diagnosis, severity, likely cause, relevant differential diagnoses and whether immediate stabilisation is required.
Specify the therapeutic objective
Decide what success means: symptom relief, eradication of infection, prevention of complications, disease control or cure.
Choose an appropriate treatment
Consider non-drug measures and select a medicine based on evidence, efficacy, safety, suitability, availability and cost.
Verify patient-specific suitability
Check allergies, previous adverse reactions, pregnancy, breastfeeding, age, weight, renal and hepatic function, comorbidities and interactions.
Write a complete prescription
Specify the generic name, formulation, strength, dose, route, frequency, duration, quantity and necessary instructions.
Explain the treatment
Discuss the purpose, administration, expected benefits, important side effects, missed doses, adherence and warning signs.
Monitor and review
Set a review point, assess response and toxicity, check investigations where indicated, and continue, adjust, switch or stop treatment.

Clinical pearl: Never start with the question, “Which drug treats this condition?” Start with, “What is wrong with this patient, what outcome do I need, and what is the safest effective way to achieve it?”

subsections.subsection_title: 1.5 The essential patient assessment before prescribing

blocks.text: A medicine that is appropriate for one patient may be dangerous for another patient with the same diagnosis.
Before prescribing, assess the following.

rows: Confirmed or working diagnosis, severity and complications
Current age and measured weight in kg where relevant
Essential for neonatal and paediatric doses; affects dosing in selected adults
Medicine, reaction, severity, timing and subsequent tolerance
Prevents re-exposure to a potentially harmful drug
Prescribed drugs, OTC medicines, herbal products, supplements and recently stopped drugs
Identifies interactions, duplication and withdrawal risks
Possibility of pregnancy, gestational age and breastfeeding
Influences medicine selection and fetal/neonatal safety
Creatinine, eGFR or calculated creatinine clearance as appropriate
Some medicines accumulate or require adjustment
Relevant liver disease, laboratory results and clinical status
Affects metabolism, toxicity and suitability of selected medicines
Asthma, ulcer disease, heart failure, epilepsy and other relevant illnesses
Electrolytes, glucose, cultures, ECG or other tests as clinically indicated
Ability to swallow, adherence, affordability, access and patient preferences
Helps select a treatment the patient can actually use

blocks.text: Medication reconciliation means establishing an accurate list of everything the patient currently uses and resolving discrepancies against the proposed treatment plan. It is especially important on admission, during transfer between wards or facilities, and at discharge.

items.text: Prescription medicines and injections.
Over-the-counter analgesics, cold remedies and antacids.
Herbal preparations and traditional medicines.
Vitamins, minerals and dietary supplements.
Medicines taken intermittently, such as sleeping tablets or migraine treatments.
Recent antibiotics, corticosteroids and anticoagulants.
Medicines recently discontinued because of an adverse effect.
Previous treatment failures and reasons for non-adherence.

blocks.text: Example: A patient admitted with acute kidney injury may report taking only prescribed medication. Further questioning reveals frequent ibuprofen use for back pain. This changes the assessment because NSAIDs can worsen renal perfusion in susceptible patients.
Do not document only “allergic to penicillin” without clarifying the reaction.

items.text: The exact medicine, if known.
The nature of the reaction.
How soon it occurred after administration.
Whether there was airway compromise, angioedema, hypotension, blistering or mucosal involvement.
Whether emergency treatment or hospitalisation was required.
Whether the patient subsequently tolerated the same or related medicines.

blocks.text: Distinguish an immune-mediated allergy from predictable adverse effects, such as nausea, and from an unexplained historical label.

A history of anaphylaxis or a severe cutaneous adverse reaction requires particular caution and appropriate specialist guidance. Do not perform an unsupervised rechallenge merely to clarify the history.

subsections.subsection_title: 1.6 How to choose the right medicine

blocks.text: When several medicines could treat the same condition, compare them systematically.
Efficacy
Does the medicine achieve the intended clinical outcome in this type and severity of illness?
Safety
What are its contraindications, major adverse effects, interactions and toxicity risks?
Suitability
Is the route, formulation, frequency and dosing schedule appropriate for this patient?
Affordability and availability
Can the patient obtain the correct quality-assured medicine and complete the intended course?
Monitoring feasibility
Can the required clinical observations, laboratory tests or drug levels be obtained?
These considerations are consistent with the principles of rational medicine use and medicines optimisation.
Prefer prescribing by generic name when appropriate, particularly in clinical records, teaching and standard treatment protocols.

A brand may be necessary when a particular formulation, delivery device, modified-release preparation or other product-specific feature is clinically important. Do not assume that products with the same active ingredient are interchangeable in every formulation.
For example, immediate-release and modified-release formulations may have different dosing schedules. Prescribing one as though it were the other can cause treatment failure or toxicity.

content_groups.group_title: When not to prescribe a medicine

blocks.text: Consider whether the patient actually needs a drug.

items.text: A self-limiting viral illness without an indication for specific drug treatment.
Antibiotics for an uncomplicated viral upper respiratory infection.
Duplicate medicines from the same therapeutic class without a clear rationale.
Continuing a medicine after its indication has resolved.
Prescribing a drug when a serious contraindication outweighs its expected benefit.

blocks.text: Non-pharmacological treatment, observation, supportive care, patient education or referral may be more appropriate.

subsections.subsection_title: 1.7 How to write a complete prescription

blocks.text: A prescription must communicate the intended treatment clearly to the dispensing pharmacist and the person administering or taking the medicine.

rows: Generic name, unless a product-specific choice is necessary
Tablet, capsule, suspension, solution, cream, injection, etc.
Amount of active ingredient per tablet, capsule, mL or other unit
Amount to be given at each administration
Oral, intravenous, intramuscular, topical or another appropriate route
Explicit schedule, such as once daily or every 8 hours
Number of days or an explicit review/stop plan
Total number of tablets, capsules, or volume to dispense
Food requirements, administration precautions or other specific directions
Name, professional registration details and signature as locally required

blocks.text: Not every prescription requires every field in exactly the same way. Inpatient medication charts, controlled-drug prescriptions and injectable orders may have additional legal or institutional requirements.

content_groups.group_title: Understanding the difference between dose, strength and quantity

blocks.text: These terms are not interchangeable.

items.text: Strength: The amount of medicine contained in a dosage unit or specified volume.
Dose: The amount of medicine the patient should receive at one administration.
Frequency: How often the dose is given.
Duration: How long treatment continues.
Quantity: The total amount supplied.

blocks.text: Consider this educational example for an adult, assuming the medicine is clinically indicated and appropriate for the patient.
ILLUSTRATIVE EXAMPLE — NOT A PATIENT-SPECIFIC ORDER
Medicine: Amoxicillin
Strength: 500 mg capsule
Dose: 500 mg per administration
Route: Oral
Frequency: Every 8 hours
Duration: 5 days, if appropriate for the confirmed indication and applicable guideline
Quantity calculation: 3 administrations/day × 5 days = 15 capsules.

The arithmetic is straightforward, but the clinical decision comes first: this example must not be used as a universal antibiotic regimen. The correct antibiotic, dose and duration depend on the infection, severity, patient factors and current treatment recommendations.
Unsafe: 0.5 mg written without a leading zero.
Safer: 0.50 mg.
The leading zero helps prevent a decimal-point error. Do not add unnecessary trailing zeros: write 5 mg, not 5.0 mg.
Unsafe: Writing only 5 mL.
Safer: Specify the intended dose in mg where appropriate, the actual product concentration in mg/mL, and the volume to administer.
The same volume can contain very different amounts of medicine in different formulations.
Unsafe: Methotrexate 10 mg daily when a once-weekly regimen is intended.
Safer: State the intended weekly schedule explicitly, with an appropriate indication, monitoring plan and counselling.
Methotrexate used for many non-oncological indications is a high-alert medicine because daily-versus-weekly errors can be fatal. Regimens differ by indication.
Unsafe: An ambiguous abbreviation or an incomplete injectable order.
Safer: Use explicit units and route, and document the concentration, diluent, final volume, administration rate and other required details.

Avoid error-prone abbreviations such as U for units, IU where it may be confused with another route, and µg where it may be mistaken for mg. Use the terminology and approved abbreviations specified by the institution.
These concepts are related but different.
A contraindication is a circumstance in which a medicine should not be used because the risk is unacceptable for the relevant patient or situation.
Contraindications may be absolute or relative, depending on the drug, the clinical circumstances and applicable product information.
A precaution is a situation requiring additional assessment, monitoring, dose adjustment or an alternative treatment. It does not automatically mean the medicine must be avoided.
An interaction occurs when one medicine changes the effect, concentration, toxicity or clinical response of another.

rows: Combined effects on the same physiological system
Opioids plus benzodiazepines can cause profound sedation and respiratory depression
One drug alters the absorption, distribution, metabolism or elimination of another
Rifampicin can reduce concentrations of many medicines through enzyme induction
Two medicines increase the risk of the same adverse outcome
NSAIDs plus anticoagulants can increase bleeding risk
Medicines jointly alter electrolytes or cardiac electrophysiology
Certain QT-prolonging drugs become more hazardous with hypokalaemia or hypomagnesaemia

blocks.text: These are illustrative examples, not exhaustive interaction rules. The actual clinical significance depends on the medicines, doses, duration and patient characteristics.

content_groups.group_title: The five questions to ask about every important interaction

items.text: What is the mechanism?
How severe is the potential harm?
Is the interaction dose-dependent or dependent on timing?
Can the combination be avoided, or does it require dose adjustment or additional monitoring?
What should be done if the patient is already taking both medicines?

blocks.text: For clinically significant interactions, our later drug monographs will identify the interacting drug, expected consequence, severity, recommended action and monitoring.
High-alert medicines have a heightened risk of causing serious harm when used incorrectly. Errors may not occur more frequently than with other drugs, but their consequences can be much more severe.
Insulin
Severe hypoglycaemia; concentration and product-selection errors.
Anticoagulants
Major bleeding or thrombosis from inappropriate dosing or interruption.
Opioids
Respiratory depression, excessive sedation and overdose.
Concentrated electrolytes
Fatal arrhythmias or other serious injury if administered incorrectly.
IV oxytocin and magnesium sulfate
Serious maternal or fetal harm if the indication, dose, administration or monitoring is incorrect.
Neuromuscular blocking agents
Paralysis and respiratory arrest; require appropriate airway and ventilatory support.

items.text: Verify the indication and patient-specific dose.
Check units, concentration and formulation independently.
Use standardised preparation and administration protocols.
Apply independent double-checks when required by local policy and when they are an effective safeguard.
Use infusion pumps and monitoring equipment where indicated.
Document administration and monitor for toxicity.
Ensure emergency equipment and reversal or rescue measures are available when appropriate.

blocks.text: Exam pearl: High-alert status does not mean a medicine is inherently inappropriate. It means the prescribing and administration process must be designed to reduce the consequences of error.

subsections.subsection_title: 1.10 The ten rights of medication administration

blocks.text: A useful safety framework for clinical practice and OSCEs is the following. The exact number and wording of the “rights” vary between institutions.
Right patient
Right medicine
Right dose
Right route
Right time
Right documentation
Right indication
Right assessment and monitoring
Right patient education
Right to refuse

These checks complement, but do not replace, clinical judgement. A correctly identified patient can still receive an inappropriate medicine if the diagnosis is wrong, the allergy history is incomplete or the prescribed dose is unsafe.

subsections.subsection_title: 1.11 Adverse drug reactions and expected complications

blocks.text: An adverse drug reaction (ADR) is a harmful, unintended response to a medicine used at an appropriate dose for a therapeutic purpose. Medication errors, overdose and inappropriate use can also cause harm, although these are not all classified as ADRs in the strict pharmacovigilance sense.

rows: Predictable from the medicine's pharmacology, often dose-related
Unpredictable and not explained by the usual pharmacological action
Osteoporosis with prolonged systemic corticosteroid use
Adrenal insufficiency after abrupt withdrawal of prolonged systemic corticosteroid treatment
Reduced anticoagulant effectiveness due to a significant drug interaction

blocks.text: This is a traditional classification used for learning. In practice, a reaction may fit more than one category.

content_groups.group_title: How to manage a suspected serious adverse drug reaction

items.text: Stabilise the patient. Assess airway, breathing, circulation, consciousness and vital signs. Treat life-threatening problems immediately.

Stop or withhold the suspected medicine when appropriate. In emergencies, do not delay stabilisation while investigating causality. Consider withdrawal risks and specialist advice for medicines that cannot safely be stopped abruptly.
Identify the reaction. Establish the medicine, dose, route, timing, concurrent medicines and relevant investigations.
Treat the complication. For example, manage anaphylaxis, hypoglycaemia, bleeding or respiratory depression according to the relevant emergency protocol.
Document and communicate. Record the reaction clearly, update the medication and allergy records as appropriate, and communicate the plan to the patient and other treating professionals.
Report when indicated. Submit suspected adverse reactions through the applicable pharmacovigilance system, including the relevant national reporting pathway in Nigeria.

blocks.text: Do not automatically label every adverse effect as a permanent drug allergy. Equally, do not dismiss a suspected severe immune-mediated reaction as a routine side effect.

subsections.subsection_title: 1.12 Monitoring treatment: before, during and after prescribing

blocks.text: Monitoring must be planned when the medicine is prescribed, not added as an afterthought.
Before treatment
Baseline assessment

items.text: Confirm the indication and severity.
Record relevant vital signs.
Check required baseline laboratory results.
Review allergies, interactions and contraindications.
Record baseline symptoms or disease markers.

blocks.text: During treatment
Efficacy and safety

items.text: Assess clinical improvement.
Check for adverse effects and toxicity.
Repeat laboratory tests at the interval appropriate for the medicine.
Assess adherence and administration technique.
Adjust the regimen when required.

blocks.text: At review or completion
Continue, change or stop

items.text: Determine whether the therapeutic objective was achieved.
Stop unnecessary treatment.
Document the intended duration and follow-up.
Provide a clear plan for recurrence, treatment failure or warning symptoms.
Reconcile the medication list at transfer or discharge.

rows: Blood pressure, renal function and potassium
INR and bleeding; review interacting medicines
Renal function and drug concentrations when indicated; auditory and vestibular toxicity
Renal function and exposure monitoring according to the treatment protocol
Full blood count, liver function and renal function according to indication and monitoring protocol
Volume status, renal function and relevant electrolytes
Clinical response, renal function, electrolytes and serum concentration when indicated

blocks.text: Monitoring intervals are medicine- and patient-specific. They will be detailed in the relevant monographs rather than assigning one interval to every patient.
Certain patients require additional safeguards because the usual adult regimen may not be appropriate.
Neonates and children

items.text: Confirm the current weight in kilograms.
Distinguish mg/kg/dose from mg/kg/day.
Verify age-specific recommendations, maximum doses and formulation concentration.
Account for neonatal gestational and postnatal age where relevant.
Double-check calculations and the final volume administered.

blocks.text: Pregnancy and breastfeeding

items.text: Consider gestational age, fetal risk and the consequences of untreated maternal illness.
Check current pregnancy-specific guidance rather than relying solely on old drug-category labels.
Assess transfer into breast milk and possible effects on the infant.
Avoid abruptly withholding essential treatment without an appropriate alternative plan.

blocks.text: Older adults

items.text: Assess renal function, frailty, falls risk and cognitive status.
Review polypharmacy, anticholinergic burden and sedating medicines.
Consider lower starting doses when justified by the drug and patient.
Review whether each long-term medicine remains necessary.

blocks.text: Renal or hepatic impairment

items.text: Determine whether the medicine or active metabolites accumulate.
Use the renal-function measure specified for that medicine.
Consider dose reduction, interval extension or an alternative medicine.
Monitor for both toxicity and inadequate treatment.

blocks.text: Important distinction: eGFR and creatinine clearance are not automatically interchangeable for drug dosing. The appropriate measure depends on the medicine's prescribing information, the guideline being followed and the patient's circumstances.

subsections.subsection_title: 1.14 Medication errors: recognition, prevention and response

blocks.text: A medication error is a preventable event that may lead to inappropriate medicine use or patient harm. It can occur during prescribing, transcribing, dispensing, preparation, administration or monitoring.

items.text: Wrong medicine or patient.
Wrong dose, unit, frequency or route.
Incorrect calculation or product concentration.
Omission of an indicated medicine.
Duplicate therapy.
Failure to account for allergy or interaction.
Incorrect dilution or infusion rate.
Failure to monitor or respond to toxicity.
Unintentional discontinuation during transfer or discharge.

content_groups.group_title: What to do if an error occurs

items.text: Assess the patient immediately and identify any imminent danger.
Stop or prevent further incorrect administration when safe to do so.
Obtain senior, pharmacy or toxicology support according to the severity.
Initiate appropriate monitoring and treatment.
Document the event and communicate honestly through the appropriate clinical process.
Report the error according to local policy and use the event to prevent recurrence.

blocks.text: Do not wait for symptoms to develop before assessing a potentially serious overdose. The required response depends on the drug, amount, timing, formulation and patient factors.

subsections.subsection_title: 1.15 Worked clinical example: reviewing a prescription

blocks.text: A 68-year-old patient with hypertension and diabetes is admitted with vomiting and acute kidney injury. The medication history includes an ACE inhibitor, a diuretic, metformin and frequent over-the-counter ibuprofen use.
What should the prescriber consider?
STEP 1 — ASSESS
Establish the patient's haemodynamic status, hydration, urine output, renal function, electrolytes, glucose and severity of illness.
STEP 2 — REVIEW THE MEDICINES

NSAID exposure may worsen renal perfusion. The ACE inhibitor and diuretic may contribute to risk during significant volume depletion. Metformin requires reassessment during acute kidney injury and serious acute illness.
STEP 3 — INDIVIDUALISE THE PLAN

Depending on the severity and clinical findings, withhold potentially contributory medicines when indicated, discontinue avoidable nephrotoxins, correct the underlying problem and use appropriate fluid management.
STEP 4 — MONITOR AND REASSESS
Follow renal function, electrolytes, fluid balance, urine output and glucose. Reassess when to restart essential chronic medicines and document the plan.

This example illustrates medication review rather than a universal order to stop every listed drug. Fluid treatment, temporary withholding and restarting medicines must be individualised to the patient's volume status, potassium, renal function, cardiovascular condition and overall clinical picture.
Use this as a final safety check before signing or authorising a prescription.

Reset checklist
This checklist is a learning aid, not a substitute for the full prescribing information, local protocols or clinical judgement.

items.text: Prescribing starts with the patient and the therapeutic objective, not the drug.
Every prescription must specify an unambiguous, appropriate regimen.
Interactions, contraindications, allergies and organ function must be considered before prescribing.
High-alert medicines and paediatric calculations require additional safeguards.
Monitoring, counselling and a clear review plan are part of the prescription.
Medication safety continues through dispensing, administration, follow-up and transitions of care.
Guide to Good Prescribing — WHO.
